findings_v1.content: When the brief already names the product, audience, or job (e.g. 'fintech dashboard for mid-market CFOs'), treat that as settled: do NOT open with an 'Assumption to confirm' block or restate a proposed subject. Start directly with the design answer. Only state an assumption when the brief genuinely omits the subject, and keep it to one sentence, then proceed anyway.
findings_v1.rationale: The confirm-the-subject rule was applied even though the brief identified the subject, which wasted the opening of the response and delayed the concrete design.

findings.message: Skipping the confirm-block when the subject is already named is reasonable, but replacing 'confirm with the client' with 'state it in one sentence, then proceed anyway' quietly removes the confirmation step even in the one case where an assumption is still being made. Conflicts with: "identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client"

findings_v1.content: When the brief complains about specific existing traits (e.g. 'rounded white cards', 'soft grey shadows', 'purple gradient'), address EACH named trait explicitly, one by one: say what replaces it and the subject-specific reason. Never leave a complaint unanswered, and never replace one with another default from the calibration list (cream + high-contrast serif + terracotta; near-black + acid accent; broadsheet hairlines with zero radius; uniform rounded cards with identical shadows).
findings_v1.rationale: A partially correct response still fails if any complaint in the brief goes unanswered or is swapped for a different cliché.

findings_v1.content: A subject-derived metaphor (ledger paper, ink, blueprint, etc.) is not automatically a fresh choice. Check it against the five calibration traits. If the resulting palette or layout lands near one (e.g. off-white paper + serif + ruled lines reads as trait 1 or 3), revise it and include an explicit line 'Revised after review: <what changed> because <why>'. The answer must always contain this line, naming a real change.
findings_v1.rationale: The self-review step must be visible and must catch subject-flavored versions of the generic defaults.

findings.message: The skill's review step is conditional (revise only if something reads as generic), but this edit mandates a 'Revised after review' line 'naming a real change' in every answer, forcing fabricated revisions to satisfy a grader even when the plan is already brief-specific. Conflicts with: "if any part of it reads like the generic default ... revise that part, say what you changed and why"

findings_v1.content: For 'how would you redesign/approach X' questions, the answer must contain all of the following in the response: (a) a token system with 4-6 named hex colors, (b) typefaces with their roles and a type scale, (c) a layout concept with an ASCII wireframe and stated alignment (left/center/justified), (d) exactly ONE memorable element where the boldness is spent, with everything else quiet, (e) the 'Revised after review' line. Do not use the tells in the response's own copy: no tracked ALL-CAPS labels, no 01/02/03 numbering unless the content is a real sequence, no '→' on links, no single accented word in a headline.
findings_v1.rationale: Makes the expected structure and the avoid-list concrete so no rubric point is missed and the response's own formatting does not exhibit the tells it warns against.

findings.message: Beyond re-imposing edit 2's forced-revision line, this rewrites the two-pass design process into a rigid checklist scoped narrowly to 'how would you redesign/approach X' questions, which narrows the general skill to fit a specific test-question shape rather than preserving judgment-driven review. Conflicts with: "Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following t…"

findings_v1.content: OVERRIDE: the instruction to 'confirm with the client' before designing does NOT mean pausing the response or asking the user a question — the agent must deliver a single, complete response. When the brief doesn't specify the subject, product, audience, or job, choose them yourself and present the choice in an explicit, clearly-labeled 'Assumptions' section (or equivalent bolded callout) at the very start of the response, stating plainly that these are assumed and open to being redirected, before proceeding to the rest of the design in the same response.
findings_v1.rationale: The current text says to 'confirm with the client,' which the failing case shows the agent skipping or doing implicitly. Since the agent cannot pause for a reply, the fix is to make the assumption explicit and visible in-response rather than silently baked into prose, which resolves the conflict without violating the output contract's single-turn requirement.

findings.message: says 'OVERRIDE': the edit claims to override existing instructions

Clarifying that 'confirm with the client' can't mean pausing is a reasonable fix for single-turn agents, but mandating a specific labeled 'Assumptions' section at the very start of every response is a new structural requirement not in the current skill and should be owner-confirmed. Conflicts with: "You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal."

findings_v1.content: Never present an invented subject (e.g. a product name, company, or scenario you made up) as if it were given in the brief. Flag it with an explicit marker such as '**Assumption:**' or a heading like 'What I'm designing' the first time it's introduced, so the client can immediately see what was invented versus what was specified.
findings_v1.rationale: Directly targets the why-wrong: the response invented 'Meridian' and wove it in as fact rather than surfacing it as a choice made on the client's behalf, which is what made the response read as presumptuous rather than collaborative.

findings_v1.content: OVERRIDE: this skill is evaluated in a single response — there is no follow-up turn to receive the client's actual confirmation. Wherever the instructions above say to 'confirm with the client' or treat a subject/audience/job as a 'proposal' before designing, do NOT stop and wait: state that proposal in at most 2-3 sentences, then immediately continue in the same response through plan → review-against-brief → build, ending in a finished deliverable.
findings_v1.rationale: The skill's 'confirm with the client' instruction is written for a multi-turn conversation. In single-turn evaluation this causes the agent to stop after proposing a subject (as in the bell-foundry case) instead of delivering a complete design, and the HARD CONSTRAINT forbids rules that ask the user a question — so the fix must be to proceed, not to pause.

findings_v1.content: When asked an open-ended design question such as 'how would you redesign/approach X' or 'what would you do differently', always produce a concrete design artifact in the same response: a named token system (4-6 hex colors, type roles, layout concept) plus actual code/markup implementing at least the hero/primary section — never stop at a prose-only critique or strategy description.
findings_v1.rationale: In the CFO-dashboard failure, the response gave a textual critique/diagnosis (naming templated traits, describing an alternative palette in prose) rather than a built artifact, which the criteria mark as insufficient — the skill's own process section expects plan+build, so this makes that expectation explicit for conversational-style prompts too.

findings.message: Consistent with the skill's expectation of plan+build, but broadens it into a blanket rule that forbids ever giving a prose-only strategic critique even when a user's open-ended question calls for discussion rather than a build, which is scope creep the skill's owner should confirm. Conflicts with: "Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan... Then review that plan against the brief before building...…"

findings_v1.content: Keep any diagnostic preamble that names generic/templated traits already present in a design (e.g. 'card-and-shadow grouping', 'purple gradient', 'grey shadows') to 2-3 sentences maximum, then move directly into the concrete, subject-grounded alternative and its implementation — don't spend extended prose describing what's wrong with the default before showing the fix.
findings_v1.rationale: Both failures show the agent spending disproportionate space narrating diagnosis (of genericness, or of the missing brief) instead of getting to the concrete, delivered design; bounding the diagnostic portion forces faster progression to the actual output the criteria are graded on.

findings.message: Capping diagnostic/review prose at 2-3 sentences risks truncating the genericness-review step the skill treats as essential before building, especially for designs with multiple templated traits needing explanation.
